So the request arithmetic is the whole of the refusal now, and it is stated as such rather than propped up by a stale second reason. Captain decision 141a keeps 8 and rewrites this justification; decision 190a raises the CAP above it and still does not move this value.
justification.minFieldRoundTrips: A hit rate is the headline number of the field leg, and one over a handful of round trips is noise wearing a percentage sign. 10 is the floor at which a single outcome cannot move the rate by more than 10 points (1/10 exactly). Below it the field is reported UNMEASURED rather than estimated. IT GOVERNS TWO DIFFERENT POPULATIONS AND BOTH ARE MEANT: entry.mjs applies it to the CLOSED round trips of the gross leg, and again to the smaller set of closed round trips whose whole window was PRICED on-chain for the net leg. The same 1/n argument fixes both, and the second is necessarily the smaller — which is the conservative side, since a net reading over too few pairs is refused rather than estimated.
justification.minFieldHitRateNet: THE SAME BAR AS minFieldHitRateGross AND THE SAME VETO, now over a real measurement instead of an upper bound (captain decision 136b). Below 0.5 the field loses money more often than not AFTER what it paid, which is conclusive; above it nothing whatsoever is established, because measured cost is itself a LOWER bound — a landing tip paid in a separate transaction of the same bundle is not in it and is not in this repo's ground truth either. So the net figure is still an upper bound on what anyone took and still cannot EARN a verdict. Re-derived from the committed tape 2026-08-02 on our own subject's create-slot outsiders, matched to the on-chain cost table, over the GATED population Stage 0's verifyOnChainCostReproduction now prices — proven create-slot openings only, the same launches scoreEntry scores: 618 closed pairs priced end to end, gross hit rate 0.7379 against a NET 0.6117, and 81 of them flip from positive to negative. Post-break alone: 460 pairs, gross 0.7630, NET 0.6478, median gross +0.1157 SOL against a median NET +0.0482. That gap is what this bar now sees and the gross bar could not. (With the unproven openings left in, which is what this check measured before 2026-08-02: 631 pairs, 0.7401 gross against 0.6070 net, 87 flips; post-break 473 pairs, 0.7653 against 0.6406. Every run prints both, so the difference is auditable rather than asserted.)
justification.maxEntryCostPerSolStaked: PINNED ON MEASUREMENT, and the measurement is the create-slot half of the same reproduction. Entry cost is a wallet's real lamport outflow in its create-slot transaction less the swap-quote SOL it committed there, so it is the fee (base and priority), the venue fee, the rent, the execution difference and any tip paid inside that transaction. THE UNIT THIS BAR IS COMPARED AGAINST IS THE PER-LAUNCH MEDIAN, not the pooled per-entry one (captain decision 140a): every scored launch contributes its own median entry and exactly one observation, so a launch with dozens of priced entrants cannot outvote a launch with one. entry.mjs computes both — entryCostPerSolStakedByLaunch is what the verdict reads, entryCostPerSolStaked is the finer-grained per-entry evidence reported beside it — and a test pins the gate to the per-launch unit. THE DENOMINATOR IS THE SEAT, NOT THE WHOLE STAKE, and the name understates that: the per-entry ratio is entryCostSol / FieldEntrant.createSlotFillSol — the entrant's own create-slot curve buy — and NOT its whole-window FieldEntrant.stakeSol. On the committed tape the two coincide for the median entrant (stakeSol / createSlotFillSol reads p50 1.000, p90 1.000, max 47.63 over 757 priced entries), and the seat is the smaller denominator, so the implemented ratio is the LARGER one and this bar is the easier one to trip — conservative, which is the direction the cost leg must fail in. Re-derived 2026-08-02 from the same population Stage 0's verifyOnChainCostReproduction prices, which since 2026-08-02 is the GATED one — proven create-slot openings only, matching what scoreEntry itself scores (data/population-tape-2026-07-29/onchain_create_slot_pnl.csv, 110 launches, 757 create-slot entries): the PER-LAUNCH median is 0.0389 SOL per SOL staked, p90 0.0985, and the WORST LAUNCH ON THE TAPE IS 0.3311; pooled over the 757 individual entries the median is 0.0369, p75 0.0812, p90 0.1970. Post-break alone (78 launches, 492 entries): per-launch median 0.0354, p90 0.0571, worst launch 0.1361; per-entry median 0.0292. Leaving the unproven openings in — the population this check used to price — reads 113 / 775 and a per-launch median of 0.0388, i.e. 0.0001 CHEAPER, which is why the gated figure is the one quoted. The bar is 0.12, and what fixes it there is the field's own gross return over that same gated population: the median closed round trip returned 0.1246 SOL per SOL staked gross (460 pairs — the same 460 minFieldHitRateGross names below). A seat priced at 0.12 therefore costs essentially the whole of the gross prize, and since gross is an upper bound the median entrant cannot clear it — that is arithmetic, not a preference. The bar sits inside the observed range rather than above it, so it is not decorative: the worst-priced launch this project has ever measured would trip it. NOTE THE DIRECTION OF THE ERROR: an out-of-transaction landing tip is NOT in the numerator, so the measured price of the seat is a LOWER bound and this bar is harder to trip than the truth warrants. That is the optimistic direction, which is why the cost leg is a gate and never a pass.
justification.minPricedFraction: 0.8 of the create-slot field must be priced on-chain before any after-cost reading may stand. This is the coverage floor behind rule 1 of the ruling — unmeasured cost is never a pass — and the failure it exists for is specific: the cost walk goes launch by launch under a per-candidate RPC ceiling, so a budget that runs out part-way leaves a cost distribution describing only the launches walked FIRST, which are the newest ones. That is a biased sample rather than a short one, and a biased sample of a cost is a wrong number. 0.8 bounds the unpriced share to a fifth. THE CEILING COSTS WHOLE LAUNCHES AND NEVER HALF OF ONE, and that is enforced at BOTH ends rather than asserted: a launch is not started unless the remaining budget covers its whole target list, and — because that reservation cannot see retries or a re-asked null getTransaction, so the ceiling can still bite mid-walk — a launch that came back short is DISCARDED whole, its partial pricing dropped and the launch counted in entry.coverage.cost.launchesDiscarded (entry.coverage.cost.launchesSkippedForBudget is the other end: launches the reservation never started, on which nothing was spent). Without the second half the bias this bar exists to bound would reappear one level down, inside a launch, where a truncated walk holds the earliest entrants by slot. It is a floor on OUR coverage and not a property of any deployer, so falling below it yields entry-cost-unmeasured — an absence of a finding, never a finding of absence.
justification.minFieldHitRateGross: A NECESSARY CONDITION, NEVER A SUFFICIENT ONE, and it can only ever take a verdict away. The fill tape is gross of fees, so this rate is an upper bound: on our own subject's post-2026-06-04 launches the screen now reads 0.763 (351 of 460 closed round trips positive, over the 86 launches whose opening is proven; the superseded reading was 0.765 over 473, taken before unproven openings stopped being scored) while the fee-inclusive record puts the whole outsider population at +0.54 SOL per launch with 51 of 106 wallets negative. Below 0.5 the field loses money before costs and therefore certainly after them, which is conclusive; above it, nothing whatsoever is established. Stage 0 asserts that this leg cannot carry a positive verdict on its own.
justification.maxCandidatesScored: 7 SINCE 2026-08-04, RAISED FROM 3 BY THE PROOF-COVERAGE LANE, AND IT IS A BUDGET BOUND RATHER THAN A STATISTICAL ONE - the same class as minLaunchesSampled, and it is documented as one because it is one. WHAT IT ANSWERS: the only full-day default run to date - the 2026-08-04 full-day default screen run record, produced by a separate lane and NOT COMMITTED IN THIS REPO, so every figure taken from it is asserted from elsewhere rather than checkable here - recorded scoringCap {max: 3, survivorsUnscored: 1} - a gate-passed wallet with 37 tokens over an 874-day span was never scored for cap reasons alone. That is a cap and not a refusal, and it is invisible in the verdict counts unless a reader opens scoringCap. WHY THE SURVIVOR COUNT CANNOT FIX THIS VALUE, stated because inventing an anchor here would be easy: the two full runs to date disagree about the gate-pass rate by nearly an order of magnitude - 4 of 82 gated (4.9%) on that 2026-08-04 full-day run, held outside this repo, against 5 of 12 (41.7%) on the elite run committed here - so at the pinned budget.maxCandidates of 195 the survivor count a run can produce spans about 10 to about 81, and no cap derived from that range means anything. WHAT DOES FIX IT is the request arithmetic, and 7 is the LARGEST cap that fits the ceilings already pinned without moving a second threshold this lane has no measurement to re-derive: 7 x maxLaunchesPerCandidate 10 x maxRequestsPerLaunch 18 = 1,260 = maxKeylessRequests, which stays under budget.maxKeylessRequests of 1,400, where 8 would be 1,440 and breach it. NOTE THE TENSION THIS LANE DOES NOT RESOLVE: budget.maxKeylessRequests' own justification calls the two ceilings independent per-client bounds that neither contains nor constrains the other, while a test orders them; staying under the lower of the two is the conservative reading, and moving either is a separate decision with its own derivation. COST, STATED HERE RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER. Stage 2's swap-api wall clock at the pinned 7s pacing goes from about 21 minutes typical / about 63 worst case to about 49 typical / about 147 worst, where typical is the modelled ~6 requests a launch. On the ACTUAL spend of the 2026-08-04 run - 168 requests over 3 candidates, i.e. ~56 a candidate - 7 candidates cost ~392 requests and ~46 minutes. THE COST LEG MULTIPLIES TOO and its per-candidate ceiling is UNTOUCHED at 500, because captain decision 197b sized that per LAUNCH and not per run: the run-level RPC worst case goes 3 x 500 = 1,500 to 7 x 500 = 3,500 requests, about 2.43 h at the serialised 2.5s pacing against about 1.04 h. A full default run's worst case therefore moves from about 16.4 h to about 19.2 h, almost all of which is still the keyless creation walk (see budget.keyedMinIntervalMs). It spends NO keyed request and no vendor allowance at any size. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not guarantee every survivor is scored and is not sized to. scoringCap.survivorsUnscored stays the reader's recourse, and the run still reports truncated with a reason when the cap bites.
justification.maxLaunchesPerCandidate: 10 against an UNMOVED minLaunchesSampled of 8, and THE GAP IS WHAT THIS VALUE BUYS (captain decision 190a, 2026-08-04). The cap is how many launches Stage 2 PLANS; the floor is how many it must SCORE. So cap minus floor is the number of planned launches a candidate may LOSE and still reach a verdict at all — to a request-cap drop, to a create slot the co-ordination rule marks nothing in (measure.mjs -> roomIsProven, decision 134a), to a window too young or unwalkable, or to any mix of them. At 10 a candidate absorbs TWO. Until 190a this value was 8, EQUAL to the floor, which absorbed NONE: one dropped launch left 7 scored and scoreEntry returned entry-unmeasured for the WHOLE CANDIDATE. That equality was never a decision — it was the coincidence of two separately-argued numbers, and nothing failed when it started costing verdicts. WHY TWO AND NOT ONE, which is the only real question here. The per-launch drop rate is MEASURED, not assumed: at the 85,000ms reach this file pins, 4 of the 127 committed launches that can show the effect exceed what maxRequestsPerLaunch affords and are dropped whole — 3.1% (seekMarginMs owns that measurement and its population). Treating a candidate's planned launches as independent draws at THAT CAUSE ALONE, the chance of finishing SHORT of the floor is 22.6% at zero spare launches, 3.1% at one, and 0.32% at two. One spare launch is therefore not enough on its own, and the independence assumption is where it fails WORST: cap-hit drops are a property of how busy a launch is, and busy launches cluster on busy deployers, so a candidate that drops one is more likely than the base rate to drop a second — and those candidates are exactly the most gate-relevant ones. Two spare launches is the cheapest gap that survives that correlation rather than assuming it away. THOSE THREE FIGURES ARE THE REQUEST-CAP COMPONENT ONLY, AND NOBODY MAY READ 0.32% AS THE FULL-DAY RUN'S EXPECTED NO-VERDICT RATE. They are computed from the 4-in-127 page-cost drop rate and from nothing else. The DOMINANT cause for a stranger is the other one named above, and this repository already measures it: census/2026-08-03-bundling-census.md reads per-launch proven at 44 of 112 = 0.3929 under the union predicate, and 0 of 13 STRANGERS proven on all eight (1 of 14 counting our own control, which is the one). At about 39% proven per launch, 8-of-10 proven is not reachable for a typical stranger, so the full-day run's no-verdict rate will be governed by roomIsProven and NOT by the 0.32% pinned here. The other half of that is honest too: this cap raise DOES help the dominant cause, since the same census recorded 3 candidates sitting at 7 of 8 that a two-launch gap now reaches — but this lane does not quantify that, and the pinned figure must not be read as if it did. THE FLOOR IS NOT THE ADJUSTABLE HALF: closing this gap by lowering minLaunchesSampled would weaken the evidence a verdict rests on rather than give it headroom, and 190a names the direction explicitly. NO BAR MOVED and no launch is scored on weaker terms — every scored launch clears exactly what it cleared at 8, and the only change is that the walk is offered two more of them, reaching two launches further back in a candidate's history. COST, STATED HERE RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER. The stage arithmetic goes 3 x 8 x 18 = 432 to 3 x 10 x 18 = 540 requests, a 25% rise carried entirely by maxKeylessRequests, which moved with it so the ceiling and the declared worst case are still the SAME number. (Both figures are 190a's own; the scoring cap has since gone 3 -> 7 and the same arithmetic now reads 7 x 10 x 18 = 1,260 - see maxCandidatesScored, which owns that raise and its cost.) maxRequestsPerLaunch is UNTOUCHED at 18 — it is under open captain decision 193c and nothing here needs it to move, because this cap multiplies that bound rather than colliding with it. Wall clock at the pinned 7s swap-api pacing, AT THE SCORING CAP OF 3 THIS DECISION WAS TAKEN AT: about 63 minutes worst case against about 50 before, and about 21 minutes typical against about 17 at the measured ~6 requests a launch. At the scoring cap of 7 pinned on 2026-08-04 the same arithmetic reads about 147 and about 49. It spends NO keyed request and no vendor allowance at any size. The COST LEG's separate exposure is re-derived and ITS CEILING MOVED WITH THIS CAP (captain decision 197b): entryCostTargets over the committed tape reads p50 19 / p90 35 / p95 41 / max 74 distinct transactions per launch, so at 10 launches a candidate costs about 190 at the median and about 350 at p90, and stage2_cost.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate went 400 -> 500 to hold the PER-LAUNCH headroom at 50 union transactions rather than let this cap cut it to 40 — 500 / 10 = 400 / 8. The median and the p90 fit inside 400 as well; what the raise consumed is the margin ABOVE them, and a launch the ceiling cannot cover is skipped WHOLE, which pushes minPricedFraction 0.8 towards entry-cost-unmeasured on exactly the busiest candidates. That entry owns the arithmetic and the measured margins. bundling_census reads this cap rather than re-pinning it, so its own derived ceiling moved 4,320 to 5,400 for the same reason. STAGE 0 WAS RE-RUN AT THIS VALUE and still refuses the known-negative control: subjectEntryRecent reads entry-room-absent over the last 10 launches, and the rolling replay reads 226 windows, 92 present, 134 absent, 0 unmeasured and 0 false positives. A CEILING THIS LANE DOES NOT CLOSE: DECOUPLING THE CAP FROM THE FLOOR CREATES A VERDICT SHAPE THAT WAS STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE AT 8-AND-8. A candidate may now be scored on 8 of 10 launches whose 2 missing launches were selected BY DROP CAUSE rather than at random - request-cap drops fall on the busiest launches, roomIsProven drops on launches with no co-ordination evidence. At 8-and-8 such a candidate returned entry-unmeasured; it now returns a verdict computed over a non-random subsample. This is the same shape the repo elsewhere refuses to read at all: the cost leg discards a ceiling-truncated launch WHOLE because a truncated walk holds the earliest entrants by slot and is a biased sample rather than a short one, and minPricedFraction exists for the same reason. THE DIRECTION OF THAT BIAS IS UNMEASURED, and the attempt that failed to settle it is the evidence rather than a hand-wave: over the 235 committed launches the rank correlation between per-launch fill count and roomLeft is 0.0250, i.e. negligible; the busiest quartile's median roomLeft is 0.3032 against the quietest quartile's 0.2771, which points one way; but dropping the busiest 7 of 235 (the 3.1% request-cap rate) moves the median roomLeft 0.3146 -> 0.3314, i.e. UP, TOWARD 'enterable', which points the other way. Two statistics, OPPOSITE IN SIGN, on n = 1 deployer: the direction is not established. What it does and does not imply: on this tape it changes no verdict, because the median roomLeft of 0.3146 sits 0.24 BELOW the minRoomLeft bar of 0.55 - but that is n = 1 and says nothing about a stranger sitting near the bar. So the standing bar ('a null result is an acceptable result, a false positive is not') is NOT DISCHARGED for this new sample shape by this lane. Captain decision 198b accepted that knowingly and split the work: a refuse-near-the-bar guard is a SEPARATE FILED LANE blocked on this one, and the full-day screen run blocks on BOTH, so the unguarded verdict shape is never what that run uses. THE REQUEST-CAP UNMEASURED RATE THIS GAP BUYS IS PINNED BY A TEST, not left implicit — test/deployer-screen.test.ts, 'THE SAMPLING RULE HAS HEADROOM, and the REQUEST-CAP unmeasured rate it buys is PINNED' — so neither this value nor minLaunchesSampled can move THAT COMPONENT silently again. It is the component and never the total: what the full-day run answers nothing at will be governed by roomIsProven, which no test here pins.
justification.maxRequestsPerLaunch: MEASURED from the committed tape's own build metadata, and the POPULATION MATTERS because the tape's windows are not all the same length. A live Stage 2 walk always reads a 60s window, and over the 210 committed launches whose stored window_ms is 60000 the pages needed per launch run p50 4, p90 6, p95 6, MAX 13. The pooled figure across all 235 covered launches — p50 4, p90 8, p95 13, MAX 24 — is inflated by the 21 of them taped over 300s (and 4 over 120s), and it is what an earlier version of this entry quoted. The cap is on REQUESTS rather than pages because the endpoint sheds ~24.7% of what it is asked for (51,715 OK against 16,960 HTTP 429 on that same build) and the client retries; counting only successes would let a launch cost 3x the printed plan. At that shed rate a page costs ~1.33 requests, and a page is only STARTED when a whole 3-request page cost still fits (i.e. at spent <= 15), so 18 requests starts ABOUT 11-12 PAGES — not the 13-14 an earlier version claimed, which counted requests the loop will not spend. WHAT THAT COVERS, STATED EXACTLY RATHER THAN ROUNDED UP: 11-12 pages is roughly double the 60s p95 of 6, but it does NOT cover that population's observed maximum of 13 — the 2 launches in 210 (1.0%) that needed 13 pages would be dropped at the mean shed rate. That is the reported failure below, not a silent one, and it is why the value does not move: raising the cap to cover a 1% tail costs the whole 7 x 10 x 18 = 1,260 stage arithmetic (3 x 8 x 18 = 432 before captain decision 190a raised the launch cap, and 3 x 10 x 18 = 540 before the proof-coverage lane raised the scoring cap to 7 on 2026-08-04), and it is under open captain decision 193c besides. THE BOUND IS EXACT RATHER THAN APPROXIMATE: a page can cost up to 3 requests (one attempt plus two backoffs), so the walk reserves the WHOLE per-page cost before starting a page and a launch therefore costs at most 18 and never 20. Checking the cap only between pages would have let a walk with one request of headroom spend three, breaking the stage arithmetic the dry run prints as the entire exposure. THE TAIL IS DROPPED, NOT TRUNCATED SILENTLY: a launch that spends the cap without reaching the mint is reported as DROPPED with its own note, and the sampling bias is stated because the launches too busy to walk are exactly the interesting ones.
justification.keylessMinIntervalMs: GOVERNS ONE HOST: swap-api.pump.fun, the fill walk, and only it. `budget.keylessMinIntervalMs` stays at 2000ms for frontend-api-v3, which has shed nothing here and must not be slowed for a fault on a different host. 7000ms is anchored on TWO INDEPENDENT READINGS OF THIS HOST. (i) LIVE: at 2000ms two consecutive Stage 2 runs against swap-api each lost 4 of the subject's 8 launches to HTTP 429 after all three attempts, so the run reported `entry-unmeasured` where the truth is `entry-room-absent`; the same code at 7000ms walked all 8 and produced `entry-room-absent`. A fast wrong answer is worth nothing, and the failure is silent in the direction that matters — a dropped launch degrades the verdict rather than announcing the pacing is wrong. (ii) THE TAPE BUILDER'S OWN RECORD against this same endpoint: the committed `window/*.meta.json` `delay` field — the adaptive delay each build settled on — reads p50 4.92s, p75 15s, p90 15.5s, max 40s, with only p10-p25 near 1.2s; and its shed share by delay quartile is 24.2% / 24.8% / 28.5% / 23.8% over the 238 builds carrying a stats block, i.e. 23.8-28.5% with the SLOWEST quartile no better than the fastest — an earlier version of this entry called that 'flat at ~24-25%', which understates the third quartile by ~4 points without changing what it establishes: backing off does not buy immunity and there is no cheap corner to sit in. 7s is therefore pinned deliberately between that p50 and p75 rather than at the bottom of the range. COST: the request arithmetic is untouched BY THIS PIN — pacing moves wall clock and never exposure — but the wall clock is not, so at the launch cap of 10 captain decision 190a set and the scoring cap of 7 the proof-coverage lane set (7 x 10 x 18 = 1,260) the typical run is about 49 minutes and the worst case about 147, and every printed estimate says so. At the launch cap of 8 this entry was written against the same pacing read about 17 and about 50, and at a scoring cap of 3 against a launch cap of 10 it read about 21 and about 63.
justification.keylessRetryBackoffMs: The tape build shed a quarter of its requests and its own recorded delay ranges from 0.75s to 40s, i.e. it backed off and retried through them. A client that treats a 429 as terminal cannot walk this endpoint at all - the first live check of the pager died on one, three launches in. Two retries at 3s and 9s clear the ordinary case, and EVERY attempt counts against both the per-launch cap and the stage ceiling, so a retry-heavy run gets a dropped launch rather than an unbounded one.
justification.tradePageLimit: 100 is what the trade endpoint serves per page and is the figure the AGENTS.md note is anchored on. Asking for less would multiply the request count for no benefit; the endpoint's own cap is what it is.
justification.windowMs: 60000 is the window_ms of 210 of the committed population tape's 239 launches — its MODAL window and not its only one: 25 were taped over 300000 and 4 over 120000, and calling it 'the tape's window_ms' (as an earlier version of this entry did) hides the 5x builds that inflate every page distribution measured across the whole tape (see maxRequestsPerLaunch). It has ONE live use — deciding a launch is old enough to have finished happening, gated by stage2.mjs on windowMs + seekMarginMs, NOT windowMs alone — plus one residual job: it is a FLOOR on the seek cursor's reach. It does NOT decide which fills are inside the measured window — windowSlotSpan does — because the mint time it would be measured from comes from the vendor and the fills come from pump.fun, and there is nothing to reconcile the two clocks with. HISTORY, read the tense: this entry used to say windowMs was used for TWO things, eligibility and PLACING the seek cursor, and that both were windowMs + seekMarginMs. Since captain decision 144a the cursor is pumpfun.mjs -> windowReachMs, derived from windowSlotSpan at a MEASURED worst-case slot rate (85000ms at the pinned values), and windowMs survives there only as the floor above. Eligibility once asked for windowMs alone, so a launch aged 60-65s passed 'old enough to have finished happening' while the newest instant the walk reaches for had not happened yet — the same tail truncation seekMarginMs exists to prevent, arriving from the future side; the sum closed that. The sum does NOT cover the measured span, and the claim that it did (160 slots is 64.0s at the nominal 400ms/slot) went out of validity when the chain slowed: at the measured 446.55ms/slot maximum, 160 slots is 71448ms and the 65000ms gate is 6448ms short. That shortfall is a known residual owned by another lane and is pinned by the test 'THE ELIGIBILITY GATE IS A SECOND BOUND AND IT IS STILL SHORT'; membership stays windowSlotSpan's alone regardless. The old assertion windowSlotSpan x 400ms <= windowMs + seekMarginMs no longer exists — it was denominated in the variable that did not move, so it stayed true and went out of validity with nothing failing. Coverage is now enforced by the describe block 'the seek cursor reaches the whole declared slot window, at a MEASURED slot rate' in test/deployer-screen.test.ts, which re-derives the slot rate from the committed tapes on every run; widening the span still fails loudly, through that block.
justification.windowSlotSpan: MEASURED, and deliberately NOT ceil(windowMs/400)=150, which is measurably too narrow. Across the 210 committed launches whose stored window_ms is 60000 the observed slot span is p50 151, p75 153, p90 155, p95 155, MAX 158 — and 51% of them hold at least one fill beyond createSlot+150 (37.1% beyond 151, 5.2% beyond 155, 0.0% beyond 160). This is not a rounding nuisance: the trailing fills are disproportionately LATE SELLS, and dropping one flips a wallet from closed to open, which shrinks fieldClosedRoundTrips — itself a gate at minFieldRoundTrips 10. So a too-narrow span silently changes gate outcomes. 160 covers 100% of observed windows with margin over the observed max of 158. THE OTHER DIRECTION, ON THE RECORD RATHER THAN AS AN OBJECTION: at the tape's observed rate (60s <-> p50 151 slots, ~397ms/slot) 160 slots is ~63.5s, so the live window is up to ~3.5s WIDER than the tape's 60s windows, and the extra late sells make realised P&L read better than the ground-truth recipe would. Because the field leg is veto-only it loosens rather than tightens — a too-generous field can only fail to veto, never earn a verdict — and the magnitude is small. THAT MAGNITUDE CLAIM IS CITED, NOT MEASURED HERE: the figure behind it (the margin sits at the thinnest part of the window, p50 18 / p95 52 fills in the last 5s) is carried over from the PR #7 review comment that recorded this tradeoff, which supplied it without naming a population, and it is reproduced nowhere in this repo — unlike the span figures above, which name theirs (the 210 committed launches whose stored window_ms is 60000). 160 was chosen on measurement, so no change is implied. WHICH OF THE TWO CONVERSIONS OF 160 SLOTS TO READ: the ~63.5s above is the TAPE'S OWN OBSERVED RATE (~397ms/slot, from 60s <-> p50 151 slots) and is SUPERSEDED by the 71448ms figure below, which converts the same 160 slots at the MEASURED WORST-CASE 446.55ms/slot. Both describe the same span and differ only in the rate; the chain's rate rose between them. Re-deriving the ~63.5s conversion and the ~3.5s-wider claim resting on it belongs to A SEPARATE LANE, so the older number is left standing rather than silently updated — read it as history, and read 71448ms as the bound anything in force is measured against. NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH ELIGIBILITY: the span is no longer what decides a launch is old enough to measure — stage2.mjs gates on windowMs + seekMarginMs (65000ms). HISTORY: this entry used to say that gate DOMINATED the span (160 slots being 64.0s at the nominal 400ms/slot) and that a test pinned windowSlotSpan x 400ms <= windowMs + seekMarginMs. Neither holds. At the measured 446.55 ms/slot maximum 160 slots is 71448ms, so the gate does NOT dominate the span — it is 6448ms SHORT of it — and that inequality was DELETED, because it was denominated in the variable that did not move: the span never changed, the chain's slot rate did, so it stayed true and went out of validity with nothing failing. The true position since captain decision 144a: the SEEK CURSOR now scales WITH this span (pumpfun.mjs -> windowReachMs), so widening the span widens the reach automatically and the span can no longer outrun the cursor; what does NOT scale is stage2.mjs's eligibility gate, which stays at 65000ms and is the known short bound. The enforcement is the describe block 'the seek cursor reaches the whole declared slot window, at a MEASURED slot rate' in test/deployer-screen.test.ts, which re-derives the slot rate from the committed tapes on every run, asserts the reach covers the whole declared span, and pins that eligibility shortfall as a measured residual. Widening the span still fails loudly, through that block. STAGE 0 DELIBERATELY DOES NOT USE THIS: it measures each committed launch over its own stored window, because the 1,502-pair reproduction against wallet_launch_pnl.csv is computed that way and that regression guard is not traded for cosmetic consistency between the two paths.
justification.seekMarginMs: The walk seeks from createdAtMs + windowReachMs = max(windowMs, ceil(windowSlotSpan x MAX_MS_PER_SLOT)) + this, i.e. 85000ms at the pinned values: a reach derived from the SPAN at a measured worst-case slot rate (MEASURED_MAX_MS_PER_SLOT 446.55 x SLOT_RATE_MARGIN 1.1 -> MAX_MS_PER_SLOT 500), with windowMs surviving there only as a FLOOR. HISTORY: before captain decision 144a the seek was createdAtMs + windowMs + this, and this margin placed the cursor; it no longer does. This margin is added ON TOP of that span-derived reach and keeps its own separate job — clock slack, so a vendor mint time running EARLY by less than 5s cannot cut the tail off the window before the slot trim ever sees it. It replaces a tail-truncation detector that could not discriminate — launches simply stop trading before the nominal window end (p50 observed span 151 against a 160 span), so any such detector fires on nearly every launch and carries no information. Designing the failure out beats reporting it. COST: the walk still pages BACKWARDS to the mint and still trims by slot afterwards, so the margin only adds rows at the newest end — about 5s of trading, roughly 30 fills at a p50 of 362 fills per window over the 210 launches taped at 60s — the population a live walk matches; pooled across all 235 covered launches the p50 is 381 and the answer is the same — i.e. at most one extra page of 100. THAT PARAGRAPH SIZES THE MARGIN ALONE AND IS NO LONGER THE WALK'S COST, which is the span-derived reach's: at 85000ms rather than 65000ms the page cost over the 127 committed launches that can show the effect goes p50 5 / p90 7 / p95 8 / max 14 to p50 6 / p90 8 / p95 9 / max 17, and 4 of 127 = 3.1% now exceed the ~16 pages maxRequestsPerLaunch affords and are dropped as request-cap, where it was 0 of 127. (That is its own measurement over its own named population and is NOT the '1% tail' maxRequestsPerLaunch cites, which is 2 launches in 210 over the 60s-taped population that structurally cannot show this gap. Do not read the two as the same number. pumpfun.mjs -> windowReachMs owns the whole page-cost story and test/deployer-screen.test.ts pins these same figures.) THE CONSEQUENCE IS THE CANDIDATE'S, NOT THE LAUNCH'S, AND THE ZERO-SLACK HALF OF IT IS NOW FIXED (captain decision 190a). When this entry was written minLaunchesSampled and maxLaunchesPerCandidate were the same pinned value (8), so there was no slack — ONE such drop among a candidate's 8 planned launches left 7 sampled and scoreEntry returned entry-unmeasured for the WHOLE CANDIDATE, a naive independent-launches ESTIMATE of 1 - (1 - 4/127)^8 = about 22.6% of candidates. The cap is now 10 against the same floor of 8, so a candidate absorbs TWO drops and the same estimate falls to about 0.32%; maxLaunchesPerCandidate owns that arithmetic and its correlation caveat, and a test pins the figure. The DROP RATE ITSELF IS UNCHANGED — this margin still costs 4 of 127 launches, and that is the number this entry is responsible for. Both estimates take their base rate from ONE deployer's long-window launches, which are also the busiest on the tape. An unmeasured verdict is 'no answer' and never a rejection, and the drop is counted and reported where the truncated tail was silent. The stage arithmetic moved with the caps and not with this margin: 7 x 10 x 18 = 1,260, where it was 3 x 10 x 18 = 540 before the scoring cap went to 7 and 3 x 8 x 18 = 432 before the launch cap went to 10. IT ALSO BOUNDS ELIGIBILITY, because it must: stage2.mjs skips a launch younger than windowMs + seekMarginMs = 65000ms, since a launch aged 60-65s has not finished happening yet. THE CURSOR IS NO LONGER WHAT THAT GATE COVERS, and the gap is a residual this lane ships knowingly: the reach is 85000ms and, at the measured 446.55 ms/slot maximum, the 160-slot span alone is 71448ms, so the gate is 6448ms SHORT of the span it is meant to cover. It is pinned as a measured residual by the test 'THE ELIGIBILITY GATE IS A SECOND BOUND AND IT IS STILL SHORT' in test/deployer-screen.test.ts, and closing it is another lane's decision. THIS IS A CURSOR HINT AND NOT A TOLERANCE: the pre-mint tripwire still compares ts < createdAtMs with ZERO slack (the measured gap is exactly 0 on all 235 committed launches) and coverage is still discharged only by the endpoint explicitly saying nothing older exists.
justification.maxKeylessRequests: Stage 2's own sub-ceiling, enforced on its own client so it cannot eat the --consistency pass's budget. 7 x 10 x 18 = 1,260 is the exact declared worst case, so no plan-level truncation is possible: the ceiling and the plan agree, and the dry run prints both. It was 432 at a launch cap of 8 and 540 at a scoring cap of 3; captain decision 190a raised the launch cap to 10 for headroom against a dropped launch and the proof-coverage lane raised the scoring cap to 7 on 2026-08-04, and this ceiling moved WITH each of them, because the two being the same number is the property that makes the dry run the whole exposure. Typical cost is far lower - at the measured p50 of 4 pages plus shedding it is about 6 requests a launch, so roughly 420 for a full run. At the pinned 7s pacing for this host that is about 49 minutes typical against about 147 minutes worst case, and the run prints both so an operator does not mistake a slow walk for a hang. A launch is only started when a full per-launch cap of headroom remains, so a run can never abandon a launch half-walked.

$comment: THE PRICE OF THE SEAT. Captain's standing ruling, 2026-08-02: fees are part of the entry
window, and 'enterable' means enterable AFTER what it costs to enter. Captain decision 136b
adds the field's AFTER-COST result, which is what stops the field leg being veto-only.
Keyless, and it spends NO vendor quota — it is Solana RPC, on the same host and the same
pacing as the creation walk. It spends no swap-api request either: every signature it prices
came free with a fill Stage 2 had already parsed.
IT RUNS ONLY WHEN THE FREE LEGS HAVE NOT ALREADY REFUSED. Room and the gross field are
arithmetic over fills in hand, so they are scored first; a deployer that fails either costs
zero RPC requests. That ordering is the whole cost model.
WHAT IT CANNOT SEE, and it must travel with every number this block produces: a landing tip
paid in a SEPARATE transaction of the same bundle is not recoverable from the entrant's own
transaction and is not measured anywhere in this repo's ground truth either. Its absence
biases the answer OPTIMISTICALLY — entry looks cheaper, and the field more profitable, than
either was. So the cost leg is a GATE and never a pass.

justification.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate: 500 SINCE CAPTAIN DECISION 197b (2026-08-04), AND WHAT IT IS SIZED AGAINST IS PER-LAUNCH HEADROOM RATHER THAN A TOTAL: 500 / maxLaunchesPerCandidate 10 = 400 / 8 = 50 union transactions a launch, so captain decision 190a's launch-cap raise leaves the cost leg exactly the room it had before it. THE MEASUREMENT UNDER IT IS UNCHANGED and is still the committed tape's, re-derived 2026-08-02 rather than copied. Distinct transactions per launch, over the 235 covered launches: the create-slot scope reads p50 7, p90 13, MAX 20 (post-break p50 7, p90 12, max 14); the whole-window scope over CLOSED create-slot outsiders reads p50 18, p90 35, MAX 70 (post-break p50 19, p90 28, max 70). The two scopes are UNIONED before anything is fetched, so a closed entrant's create-slot transaction is paid for once, AND THE UNION IS WHAT MUST BE COSTED: re-running entryCostTargets as the code calls it over those 235 launches gives p50 19, p90 35, p95 41, MAX 74 distinct transactions per launch — not 7 + 18. At maxLaunchesPerCandidate 10 that is about 190 requests at the median, ~350 at p90 and ~740 at the observed worst; at the 8 this entry was first written against it read ~152 / ~280 / ~592. THE INTERACTION THAT MADE THE RAISE NECESSARY, named here because the earlier version of this entry argued only that the median and the p90 still fitted: stage2.mjs skips a WHOLE launch when the remaining per-candidate ceiling cannot cover its target list — a launch is never priced half-way — and entry.mjs then returns entry-cost-unmeasured if the priced share falls below minPricedFraction 0.8. THAT SHARE IS A HIT RATE OVER FIELD ENTRANTS, NOT OVER LAUNCHES (entry.mjs -> entryCostPriced = hitRate(field, e => Number.isFinite(e.entryCostSol))), and a launch skipped for budget is by construction one of the heaviest, so it removes a disproportionate share of the numerator while every one of its entrants stays in the denominator. TWO DIFFERENT QUANTITIES LIVE IN THIS PARAGRAPH AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME NUMBER. The first is the PER-PLANNED-LAUNCH HEADROOM, ceiling / maxLaunchesPerCandidate, which is the captain's sizing metric and is held CONSTANT by the raise at 500 / 10 = 400 / 8 = 50 requests a planned launch — that is why 500 and not another number. The second is the BREACH POINT, the sustained per-launch cost at which the priced share first falls under minPricedFraction, which on a LAUNCH-COUNT reading is ceiling / ceil(minPricedFraction x cap): 400 / ceil(0.8 x 8) = 400 / 7 = 57.1 transactions a launch at the old cap of 8, 400 / ceil(0.8 x 10) = 400 / 8 = 50.0 at the cap of 10 with the ceiling left at 400, and 500 / 8 = 62.5 at 500. So the raise does not merely restore the old 57.1, it exceeds it; an earlier version of this entry printed ~58 for both ends and understated what 500 buys. ALL THREE OF THOSE ARE UPPER BOUNDS ON THE TRUE BREACH POINT, and the direction of the approximation is known rather than guessed: minPricedFraction gates on entryCostPriced, which is hitRate(field, e => Number.isFinite(e.entryCostSol)) — a share of FIELD ENTRANTS and not of launches. A launch skipped for budget is by construction one of the heaviest, so it carries more entrants than average and takes a larger share of the numerator than the launch-count arithmetic assumes, while every one of its entrants stays in the denominator. The entrant-weighted breach point therefore bites EARLIER than 57.1 / 50.0 / 62.5, and this repository holds no measured value for it — stated as an unmeasured optimistic gap rather than filled in with an invented figure. THE MEASURED MARGINS, so the number's provenance is honest rather than asserted. Replaying entryCostTargets as the code calls it over the committed tape (235 launches, 226 ten-launch windows) under stage2.mjs's greedy skip: the 400 ceiling was NEVER reached at either cap — 0 of 226 windows skipped a single launch — and the worst ten-launch window cost 350 of 400 against the worst eight-launch window's 316, i.e. headroom 84 at a cap of 8 falling to 50 at a cap of 10. WHY 500 DESPITE THE TAPE NEVER BREACHING 400, which is the captain's reasoning and is recorded as such: that margin evidence is n = 1 deployer while a full-day run screens STRANGERS, and the observed maximum of 74 transactions on a single launch already sits above the ~50 sustained breach point a cap of 10 at 400 would have created. An unmeasured cost is never a pass, so the failure this avoids is a NULL result rather than a false positive — but it is exactly the no-verdict outcome decision 190a exists to reduce, re-introduced on the busiest and therefore most gate-relevant candidates. An earlier version of this entry printed 200 / 380 / 700, which is the same arithmetic with the union left out (the plain sums 25 / 48 / 90 x 8); it overstated the cost by ~30% and the conclusion survives under either reading. The ceiling covers the median and the p90 whole and truncates only a pathological candidate, and it truncates VISIBLY: a launch is never priced half-way, so the ceiling costs whole launches and entry.coverage.cost records how many. THE NEW COST, stated here rather than discovered later: at the pinned 2.5s that is about 8 minutes per candidate at the median (190 requests at the cap of 10; it was ~6 at 152 requests under the cap of 8, and the ~8 an earlier version printed was the un-unioned 200) and about 21 at the ceiling, and at the maxCandidatesScored of 7 pinned on 2026-08-04 the declared worst case is 7 x 500 = 3,500 RPC requests and about 146 minutes (it read 3 x 500 = 1,500 and about 62.5 minutes at the scoring cap of 3, against 3 x 400 = 1,200 and about 50 minutes before this ceiling moved). The dry run prints it. The realistic cost is far lower because only candidates that survive room AND the gross field are priced at all — at the scoring cap of 3 the committed live run had one such candidate of three, and the same fraction at a cap of 7 is what a run actually pays.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: INHERITED FROM creation_walk.rpcMinIntervalMs AND NOT AN INDEPENDENT CHOICE — api.mainnet-beta rate-limits GLOBALLY across getSignaturesForAddress, getTransaction and getBlock, so this leg and the creation walk draw on one allowance. 2,500ms is that block's measured figure: 1,400ms is the documented floor but a 200-request run at that pace took over 890 seconds instead of 280 because the endpoint was shedding and the backoff was paying for it. The two legs are SERIALISED rather than run beside each other for the same reason: two concurrent jobs earned a sustained 429 lockout. Batching is not used here either — measured actively harmful on this host, 58s at batch=1 with zero shed events against 110s at batch=8 with eleven.
justification.preferBlockRoute: getBlock(slot, transactionDetails='full') returns EVERY transaction in the create slot in one request, collapsing the create-slot scope from ~7 requests a launch to 1. It is UNTESTED against this endpoint from this repo — what is known is that getBlock works here for signature listing; what is unknown is whether the public endpoint serves full blocks to this client and what a busy mainnet slot's payload costs. So it is probed BEHIND A FALLBACK: anything other than a usable block latches the candidate onto the per-signature route, and the route that ran reaches the run record so a saved run says which one paid for its numbers. It buys request count and NOTHING ELSE — in particular it does not reach out-of-transaction landing tips, because attributing a sibling transaction in the same slot to the same bundle is an inference the chain does not support. Set false to pin the walk to the proven route.

$comment: Hard bounds, enforced in code. There is no flag that disables one.
CAPTAIN'S INSTRUCTION, 2026-08-02: 'There is no current free method to save on the madeonsol
key request limits ... use all free tier daily quota as needed if it gets results.' These
bounds are therefore the FULL Free-tier daily allowance (~200 requests/day), not a fraction
of it. An earlier quarter-allowance ceiling of 45 was this tool's own caution, never a
captain instruction, and it is WITHDRAWN — do not reintroduce it or re-derive it: there is no
free substitute for this data, so an unspent allowance buys nothing and only leaves questions
unanswered.
The conditional binds: 'if it gets results'. This authorises sizing a run by what the
question needs. It does NOT authorise sweeping, idle retrying, or re-running to re-evidence a
side observation. A run that cannot say in advance what it will answer does not get the
allowance.
SCOPE: this relaxation is MadeOnSol ONLY. The SolanaTracker / CoinGecko keys are shared with
production and the standing 'do not waste the quota that is production quota too' is
unchanged, as is the keyless pump.fun pacing below, which bounds a shared public resource for
an entirely different reason.
HELIUS IS NO LONGER IN THAT LIST (captain, 2026-08-03): its key is UNSHARED and belongs to
this research lane alone, so the whole 10M monthly allowance is this tool's and no other
consumer can be starved by a heavy run. It is metered on its own terms in
creation_walk_helius, in CREDITS rather than requests, because that is what the vendor bills.
The burst limit is NOT relaxed either: ~10/minute is a rate the vendor enforces, not a
self-imposed caution, so keyedMinIntervalMs stays.

justification.maxKeyedRequests: 200 is the whole Free-tier daily allowance as measured (see tools/deployer-screen/README.md). Enumeration costs 3 (recent-bonds, alerts, leaderboard) and the gate costs 1 per candidate, so the 195-candidate cap costs 198 worst case and the remaining 2 are the retry headroom. A run whose PLANNED worst case exceeds this is refused before its first request rather than allowed to die part-way through. STAGE 2 ADDS NOTHING TO THIS: it reuses the profile Stage 1 already fetched and spends no keyed request of its own.
justification.maxCandidates: 195 = 200 - 3 enumeration - 2 retry headroom, i.e. the cap is whatever the allowance leaves rather than a judgement about how many deployers are worth grading. It is also well above what the three enumeration queries can surface (50 + 50 + 50 rows, heavily overlapping and then pre-filtered — screen.mjs caps the page limit at 50 and seed.mjs then clamps alerts to the same 50, so the vendor's 100-row alerts ceiling is never asked for; both committed runs show 50, and an earlier version of this entry read 50 + 100 + 50, which overstates what enumeration can reach and therefore understates the headroom), so the DEFAULT run grades everything it surfaces and coverage truncation becomes the exception it is supposed to be.
justification.keyedMinIntervalMs: Free tier bursts at ~10/minute. 6.5s between request starts keeps a run under that with margin, and margin matters because the allowance is shared. This is the vendor's rate limit, not our caution, so raising the daily bounds does not touch it. A full 198-request run therefore takes about 21 minutes, which is the intended cost of respecting the burst limit — but THAT IS NO LONGER THE RUN'S WALL CLOCK AND MUST NOT BE READ AS ONE. The default history source is creation-derived, and the Solana RPC walk dominates everything else by an order of magnitude: 195 candidates x 100 requests x 2.5s is ~13.5 HOURS on its own. Add ~21 minutes keyed, ~26 for the gate's ownership listing on frontend-api-v3, ~147 for Stage 2 on swap-api (7 x 10 x 18), up to ~146 more for Stage 2's cost leg (stage2_cost, 7 x 500 requests at the same 2.5s, and it SHARES this limiter rather than adding a second queue), and a further ~19.5 with --consistency, and a full default run at the candidate cap is ABOUT 19.2 HOURS end to end, or ~19.5 with --consistency. Those two legs multiplied when the scoring cap went 3 -> 7 on 2026-08-04; stage2_entry.justification.maxCandidatesScored owns that raise and its cost, and this entry only carries the total. An earlier version of this note said 47 minutes; it predated the creation walk and was wrong by a factor of twenty. DO NOT KILL A DEFAULT RUN FOR STILL GOING AFTER AN HOUR. The liveness signal is not the same on every leg: the keyed and frontend-api-v3 clients print one line per request, but the creation walk would emit ~20,000 of those, so it prints a PERIODIC HEARTBEAT — the first request of each candidate and then every tenth, i.e. a line roughly every 25 seconds at this walk's 2.5s pacing, showing that candidate's spend against maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate. Watch that counter rather than expecting a line per request, and use --candidates N to bound the run (the RPC leg is N x 100 x 2.5s) or --ownership-only to skip the walk entirely for a fast pass whose bias towards rejection is stamped into the record. renderDryRun prints this arithmetic for whatever flags are actually passed.
justification.keylessMinIntervalMs: GOVERNS ONE HOST: frontend-api-v3.pump.fun — the gate's ownership listing and the --consistency creator walk, which share one client. It does NOT govern the Stage 2 fill walk, which has its own pinned pacing (`stage2_entry.keylessMinIntervalMs`) because it reaches a different host that behaves differently. THIS VALUE IS A CONSERVATIVE CARRY-OVER, NOT A MEASUREMENT OF THE ENDPOINT IT GOVERNS, and the correction matters: the ~0.5 requests/second figure this was originally justified by was measured against api.mainnet-beta.solana.com, and the June report's own spend table records BOTH swap-api.pump.fun and frontend-api-v3.pump.fun as NOT CONTACTED — so it was never a pump.fun measurement at all. It is kept because it is conservative and because frontend-api-v3 has shed nothing in this tool's use of it; if that host is ever measured, this number should be re-derived from that measurement rather than from a different host's. Either way it bounds a shared public resource rather than expressing our own caution, so the MadeOnSol relaxation does not touch it. The RETRY COUNT is a separate question and is not this bound: a keyless request is retried on a 429 or a 5xx, and each attempt counts against maxKeylessRequests.
justification.maxKeylessRequests: A PER-CLIENT CEILING, NOT A RUN TOTAL, and the distinction is what the code enforces: screen.mjs builds TWO independent keyless clients, and this value bounds only the general one (frontend-api-v3). Stage 2 runs on its own client under its own `stage2_entry.maxKeylessRequests` of 1,260, which this number neither contains nor constrains, so the enforced combined worst case is 1,400 + 1,260 = 2,660 requests (it was 1,400 + 540 = 1,940 before the proof-coverage lane raised the scoring cap to 7 on 2026-08-04, and 1,400 + 432 = 1,832 before captain decision 190a raised the launch cap to 10). 1,400 is sized to COVER the candidate cap rather than to bound it, and it is sized for what the code now actually spends on this client, which is TWO passes and not one. The GATE reads the ownership listing it merges the creation window with, up to 4 pages PER CANDIDATE (screen.mjs LISTING_PAGES_FOR_MERGE); the --consistency pass then costs up to 3 pages per gate SURVIVOR, and every candidate can be one. So 195 candidates cost 195 x 4 = 780 for the gate plus 195 x 3 = 585 for consistency = 1,365 worst case, and the remaining 35 are the retry headroom. The earlier 600 was justified on the consistency pass alone and was already exceeded by gating at the default candidate cap. A keyless ceiling below the plan would make the tool stop looking part-way through a run it had already paid for in KEYED quota, and an unmeasured candidate is not a measured one — so screen.mjs now also REFUSES a plan whose keyless worst case does not fit, before its first request, exactly as it does for the keyed one. Raising the count does not lean harder on pump.fun — keylessMinIntervalMs is unchanged, so what it buys is wall-clock time and nothing else: 1,365 requests at 2s is ~45.5 minutes, of which ~26 is the gate's own 780 pages. That is a minority of the run's wall clock rather than the whole of it — see keyedMinIntervalMs, where the creation walk's ~13.5 hours puts a full default run at ABOUT 19 HOURS (13.54 h RPC + ~21 min keyed + ~26 min gate listing + ~147 min Stage 2 + ~146 min the cost leg = 19.2 h; Stage 2's leg was ~63 min and the cost leg ~62.5 min at the scoring cap of 3, so the proof-coverage lane's cap of 7 adds ~2.8 h to what was a 16.42-hour run. An earlier version of this sentence said 15 and contradicted the total four lines above it). The June report sustained 460 consecutive keyless requests at 1.4s apart with zero shedding. These are pump.fun's free endpoints — no key, no vendor allowance, and no shared quota is touched by any of it.

$comment: Bounds for the creation-derived launch history — the walk that answers 'which tokens did this
wallet CREATE' instead of 'which tokens does it OWN NOW'. See creation.mjs for why the two
differ and for the on-chain observation that established it.
This walk is the expensive part of a run by an order of magnitude, because the only keyless
index that reaches a create transaction is the wallet's own signature index, and for a pump.fun
deployer that index is dominated by strangers' failed trades. Every bound here is therefore a
hard ceiling, and readCreatedHistory reports which one bit rather than truncating silently.
The walk covers a CONTIGUOUS WINDOW BACKWARDS FROM NOW. Inside it every creation is found;
outside it none is, and mergeHistories falls back to the ownership listing and says so. A
create count read as a lifetime figure under any stopReason other than 'index-exhausted' is
wrong in the same direction as the vendor's sliding 'lifetime' window.

justification.maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate: Measured 2026-08-02: sustained keyless throughput against api.mainnet-beta is about 0.42 transactions/second, i.e. roughly one request per 2.4s including backoff, and a create is found by inspecting every SUCCEEDED signature in the wallet's index. The success fraction varies enormously between deployers — 1.7% on the busiest wallet screened, 99.7% on another — so the cost of a full history ranged from 7 minutes to 84 hours across the 12 wallets of runs/2026-07-29-elite.json. 100 requests is a per-candidate ceiling that keeps a 12-candidate run inside about 50 minutes; on a quiet wallet it is the whole history, on a busy one it is a window of hours and the record says so. NOTE THE OTHER END OF THAT ARITHMETIC: at the 195-candidate cap it is 19,500 requests and ~13.5 HOURS, which is the dominant cost of a default run — --candidates N is the lever that bounds it, and --ownership-only skips it for a fast pass whose bias is stamped into the record. See CREATION-DERIVED.md for the per-wallet costs.
justification.maxSignaturePages: 200 pages is 200,000 signatures, past which no keyless walk is finishing inside a session. It exists so a wallet with an enormous index cannot turn the request ceiling into the only brake.
justification.maxTransactionsPerCandidate: A BACKSTOP THAT CANNOT CURRENTLY BIND, and there is no measurement behind the number. pumpfun.mjs stops the walk at transactionsInspected >= this, but a transaction is inspected one getTransaction at a time (txBatchSize 1) from a client capped at maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate 100, so AT MOST ~100 transactions can ever be inspected for one candidate — 8000 is unreachable by a factor of ~80, and every real walk stops on 'request-ceiling' or 'index-exhausted' instead. It is kept rather than deleted so that raising the request ceiling does not silently remove the only bound on inspection work, and it is documented as unjustified rather than given a manufactured anchor: what would justify a value is a measured cost per inspected transaction against a wall-clock budget, which only exists for the REQUEST ceiling (see maxRpcRequestsPerCandidate, 0.42 tx/s measured 2026-08-02). Delete it or re-derive it if the request ceiling ever rises above it.
justification.txBatchSize: 1, and the 1 is measured. report.md 9.4 recorded batches of 5-8 getTransaction as sustainable, and that no longer holds: on 2026-08-02, fetching the same transactions at batch=1 took 58s with ZERO load-shed events, batch=4 took 76s with 7, and batch=8 took 110s with 11. Throughput was 0.42 tx/s at batch=1 and 0.36 tx/s at batch=8 — the endpoint weights each entry of a JSON-RPC batch against its limiter, so a batch of 8 spends 8 tokens and buys nothing but backoff. Batching is therefore actively harmful HERE TOO, exactly as it is on pump.fun's keyless endpoints. The client still supports batching, capped at 8, because the endpoint's behaviour is the vendor's to change and re-measuring is cheaper than rebuilding.
justification.rpcMinIntervalMs: 1,400ms is the documented floor, but a 200-request run at that pace on 2026-08-02 took over 890 seconds instead of the expected 280 — the endpoint was shedding load and the retry backoff was paying for it. 2,500ms is the observed rate at which that stops happening, so it is faster in wall-clock than the nominally quicker setting. api.mainnet-beta rate-limits GLOBALLY across getSignaturesForAddress and getTransaction, and two concurrent jobs earned a sustained 429 lockout, so this is one queue with one request in flight.

$comment: CREATION ENUMERATION, PRIMARY SURFACE. Captain decision 156a, 2026-08-03. The same question
creation_walk and creation_walk_helius answer — 'which mints did this wallet CREATE' — read
off Dune's decoded pump.fun creation events instead of walked out of a signature index.
tools/deployer-screen/dune.mjs owns the method; CREATION-DERIVED.md section 8 owns the
reproduction and the measured cost.
THE SURFACE IS A UNION AND THE UNION IS NOT NEGOTIABLE: pump_evt_createevent UNION
pump_call_create, deduped by mint. pump_call_create ALONE returns ZERO rows for our subject
(it decodes only the original Create; this deployer uses CreateV2). pump_call_create_v2 ALONE
is not backfilled before ~2026-04-28 and silently misses 101 of our 239 launches, `maxxing`
included. Attribution keys on "user"/account_user, the SIGNER — never on `creator`, which is
a settable CreateV2 argument that six bot-signed mints use to name our subject, inflating the
EVERY DUNE-DERIVED COUNT SHIPS WITH ITS OWN COVERAGE PROBE, and that is the binding condition
of the decision rather than a nicety. Decoded tables have SILENT START DATES: they return a
confident, well-formed, complete-looking answer that is simply wrong before their first row,
with nothing in the response saying so. Same failure shape as a truncated backwards walk in
pumpfun.mjs and the same direction: plausible and silent. dune.mjs -> assessCoverage refuses
a reading that reaches outside the probe, and a refused reading FALLS BACK to the walk — it is
never published as a measured count.
SPEND. Free tier, 2,500 credits/month, SHARED with whatever else holds the key. What a run
may spend against that allowance is CHECKED BEFORE ITS FIRST REQUEST — dune.mjs ->
checkDuneAllowance, and README.md -> 'The monthly credit ceiling' owns it — but nothing here
carries state ACROSS runs, so the arithmetic between them is still the operator's.
A FAILED EXECUTION IS STILL BILLED AND IS TERMINAL: client.mjs -> DuneClient never retries
one, and no code may wrap a retry around it. Budget from BILLED credits, not
execution_cost_credits, which understates by ~3.5x because retrieving results is ~71% of the
bill at ~20 credits/MB.

justification.creationQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved query the enumeration executes, pinned so a run names the surface it read. dune.mjs -> CREATION_SQL holds that query's SQL byte for byte and assertSavedQueryMatches compares the two BEFORE spending an execution, so a saved query edited from a browser fails the run loudly instead of returning a different measurement under the same name. Reused rather than created: it is the query `slot-zero-dune-evaluate` section 7 (held in firstmate's records, not in this repo) designates as the production shape, upgraded in place from event-only to the union, because the free tier allows only 10 private queries and the account holds 10. THEREFORE EVERY CHANGE TO CREATION_SQL IS A DEPLOY STEP AGAINST THIS QUERY ID: saved query 8204672 must be edited in place to the committed text before the next real run, because the comparison happens BEFORE the execution and a mismatch is not a wrong answer — it is a terminal refusal of the whole Dune leg on every run until they agree. There is no new query slot to create. tools/deployer-screen/README.md -> 'Deploying a change to the committed SQL' owns the step.
justification.coverageQueryId: NOT A THRESHOLD — the saved coverage probe, pinned for the same reason and verified the same way against COVERAGE_SQL. It is the scout's own coverage query (report.md section 2) widened to carry min/max block time beside the monthly counts. It probes THREE tables while the enumeration reads TWO: pump_call_create_v2 is included precisely so the probe's own output demonstrates the boundary that disqualifies it, rather than this file asserting it in prose.
justification.maxExecutionsPerRun: 2, and the 2 is the exact plan rather than a round number: one execution for the enumeration, and at most one more to re-execute the coverage probe when the cached one has gone stale. Nothing else in a run may execute. An execution is BILLED WHETHER OR NOT IT SUCCEEDS and is never retried, so this is the bound on the only unrecoverable spend the Dune leg has. MEASURED 2026-08-03 on this account: the enumeration of 5 wallets / 482 rows cost 0.919 execution credits and 1.919 billed; the coverage probe cost 0.751 execution credits and 0.751 billed. AT THE 195-CANDIDATE CAP the execution cost barely moves — scan cost is nearly independent of how many wallets are in the filter, measured at 5 and at 20 — and what scales is bytes returned, which maxResultRows bounds. THIS BOUNDS ONE RUN, and it is what the monthly credit guard prices that run against: worstCaseCreditsPerExecution x this value is the compute half of the plan checkDuneAllowance compares with the account's remaining balance before the first request. The tool is still stateless BETWEEN runs, so the arithmetic across them stays the operator's. That limit is stated rather than papered over.
justification.maxRequestsPerRun: Requests bound the WALL CLOCK and the polite use of a shared host; maxExecutionsPerRun bounds the money, and the two are separate ceilings because a poll loop that spent an execution's worth of budget on status checks would be counting the wrong thing. The arithmetic: each of the two possible executions costs 1 SQL-verification GET + 1 execute + up to maxPollAttempts 40 status polls + 1 results read = 43, so 2 x 43 = 86, plus the credit guard's single POST /usage and its one retry = 88, and the remaining 12 are the retry headroom (every read is retried at most once, and each attempt counts). 100 covers that sum. MEASURED: both executions on 2026-08-03 completed in 6-9 s, i.e. 2-3 polls, so a real run spends about 8 requests and the ceiling is a backstop rather than a budget.
justification.maxResultRows: 20,000 rows, and THE UNIT THAT MATTERS IS BYTES rather than rows, because results are billed at ~20 credits/MB and that is ~71% of the bill. TWO BOUNDS HOLD NOW AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT BOUNDS. (1) THE BYTES BOUND, unchanged: every result read is issued with `?limit=maxResultRows`, so no read can return more rows than this whatever the query does. MEASURED 2026-08-03 at FOUR columns: ~97 bytes/row (482 rows, 46,718 bytes), and RE-MEASURED 2026-08-05 at the SIX columns CREATION_SQL selects today — `launches_total`, which makes the per-deployer cap below detectable instead of silent, and `is_mayhem_mode`, captain decision 227a's recorded-and-reported flag. The six-column shape reads 105.92 bytes/row batch-shaped (51,691 bytes over 488 rows, five wallets) and 105.91 for a single wallet (26,690 over 252), so <=121 bytes/row still holds, i.e. <=~2.42 MB and ~48 credits for a read that fills this ceiling. It is no longer an arithmetic bound over an unobserved column — but its headroom is now thinner than one more column is worth, and CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.2c owns the figures and what a seventh column must do before it is added. (2) THE ROWS BOUND, new: CREATION_SQL returns at most greatest(500, floor(19999 / <deployers in the batch>)) rows PER DEPLOYER — 19,999 being this value minus one, and 500 a pinned floor, both written as literals in the SQL because a saved Dune query cannot read this file, and both guarded by a test that fails if they stop agreeing with this file. So a run's rows are bounded at max(19,999, <deployers> x 500), which ABOVE 39 DEPLOYERS EXCEEDS THIS CEILING — and a result that does is refused whole by the reader below, exactly as it was before the cap existed, rather than published. It is NOT a by-construction bound and must not be quoted as one; the arithmetic a given run applies is visible in the dry run. WHY THE FLOOR: a purely derived cap is 102 rows at the 195-candidate cap, which would truncate the subject deployer (247 launches, the reproduction control) and 4q4GKBpV (152) on every full run — a systematic per-wallet failure biased towards the largest and most gate-relevant wallets, which is worse than the rare all-or-nothing one it replaced. 500 is ~2x the largest per-wallet history this repo has measured (8/10/65/152/247, CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.3), so NO measured deployer is capped at any batch size, and ~17x below the industrial-spam extreme (8,518 deploys), so a spam wallet is still contained. WHY THAT SECOND BOUND EXISTS: this ceiling refuses the WHOLE RESULT, and enumeration is ONE execution for the whole batch, so before the cap a single industrial-spam deployer (README records an 8,518-deploy wallet reachable from the total_bonded leaderboard, one of the three seeds) carried every other candidate past it and sent the entire run to the RPC walk — ~13 hours of walking traded against ~1 credit of Dune, decided by one outlier. The cap moves that refusal onto the wallet that earned it: a deployer whose true count exceeds its share is detected exactly (declared count above rows returned), refused with a reason, and walks alone. THE CEILING IS KEPT AS THE BACKSTOP rather than deleted, and under the 500 floor it stays genuinely REACHABLE: roughly 40 wallets of 500+ launches in one batch (the total_bonded leaderboard seed can serve them) put a result past it, and that run falls back whole exactly as merged main already did — never worse than today, just not eliminated. Reaching it otherwise means the cap did not apply — a saved query edited past the committed text, or a shape the reader does not understand — and a soft bound on a billed read is not a bound. WHAT A REAL RUN COSTS AGAINST IT: at the 195-candidate cap and a median deployer history of ~50 launches, ~9,750 rows is ~0.95 MB, about 20 credits — roughly 125 full-cap runs a month, unchanged by the cap because a median-shaped batch never approaches it. The ceiling REFUSES rather than pages: an unbounded read is an unbounded bill, and a paged one would spend the allowance discovering how big the answer was. RAISING THIS VALUE MOVES THE DERIVED HALF OF THE PER-DEPLOYER CAP WITH IT (the 500 floor is separate and moves only on its own evidence), so the SQL literals and the saved Dune query 8204672 all have to move in the same commit — see creationQueryId.
justification.pollIntervalMs: 3,000 ms between status polls. MEASURED 2026-08-03: the two executions finished in 6 s and 9 s, so a run polls two or three times. Polling faster would buy at most a couple of seconds against a leg that replaces a walk measured in hours, and it is a shared free-tier host. Polling is a READ and costs no execution credit, but every poll counts against maxRequestsPerRun, which is what stops a slow execution turning into an unbounded loop.
justification.maxPollAttempts: 40 polls at 3,000 ms is 120 s, against the 6-9 s the two committed executions actually took — roughly 13x the observed worst. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE, and it is stated as an operational bound rather than dressed up: nothing in this repo measures the tail of Dune execution latency, because two executions is not a distribution. What would justify a value: execution durations over a month of scheduled runs, which the run record's dune block will accumulate. The failure direction is the safe one — running out of polls abandons the Dune leg and falls back to the RPC walk, and the execution is billed either way, so the cost of being wrong here is bounded by one execution.
justification.minIntervalMs: 250 ms between request starts, and NO MEASUREMENT OF THIS HOST BACKS IT. It is a courtesy floor on a free tier, carried across from creation_walk_helius.rpcMinIntervalMs (200 ms, which WAS measured, on a different vendor) and rounded up rather than down. A real run issues about 8 requests, so the pacing costs ~2 s of a run measured in minutes and buying a measurement of it would be spending a shared allowance to tune something that is not a cost. What would justify a value: a pacing ladder against Dune's status endpoint recording shed events per rung, which is exactly what was done for Helius and has not been done here.
justification.maxCoverageLagMs: 6 hours. The probe cannot vouch for a period it does not reach, and the recent end is precisely where a live screen looks — a deployer that launched this morning is the one a discovery feed just surfaced. Dune's own freshness was measured by the scout at ~3-4 minutes (report.md section 6, item 8), so 6 hours is about 100x the vendor's lag and is not a tight bar; what it actually bounds is OUR cache, since the probe defaults to a cached read that could be arbitrarily old. THE FAILURE IS REPAIRED RATHER THAN INHERITED: when staleness is the ONLY thing wrong, dune.mjs re-executes the probe once, which is the second of the two budgeted executions. A structural refusal — a missing table, a month with no rows — is not retried, because asking the same question again returns the same answer.
justification.worstCaseCreditsPerExecution: 25 credits, the WORST case one of this leg's executions may cost, and it is the input the monthly-ceiling guard converts a plan into money with (client.mjs -> estimatePlanCredits). It has to be pinned per lane because DUNE PUBLISHES NO PRICE TABLE FOR EXECUTION COMPUTE — the evaluation lane recorded exactly that, and the cost depends entirely on what the statement scans. MEASURED on this account, 2026-08-03, for THESE two queries: the enumeration 0.919 execution credits and the coverage probe 0.751, and scan cost is nearly independent of how many wallets are in the filter (measured at 5 and at 20). The widest execution any slot-zero lane has recorded that does NOT join the trade tape is 19.25 credits (a curated-schema table listing, `slot-zero-launch-venue-daily-rates` section 7, held in firstmate's records, not in this repo); the two that DID join `dex_solana.trades` cost 81.74 and 221.51, which is why the figure is a per-lane pin and not a repository constant. 25 is ~27x the measured cost of the queries this leg actually runs and just above the widest non-trade-join execution on record. NEITHER QUERY MAY GROW A TRADE JOIN WITHOUT MOVING THIS NUMBER: CREATION_SQL and COVERAGE_SQL read the decoded create surfaces only, and a statement that reached the trade tape would be ~9x this pin with nothing else failing.
justification.resultBytesPerRowCeiling: 121 bytes per result row, UNCHANGED at SIX columns and, for the first time, backed by a measurement of the production shape rather than by arithmetic over an unobserved column. It is pinned here because the credit guard needs it as a number, and a bound that exists only in a sentence cannot be arithmetic. HISTORY: measured 2026-08-03 at FOUR columns, ~97 bytes/row (482 rows, 46,718 bytes); the fifth, launches_total, was then bounded by ARITHMETIC at <=24 bytes, and that is where 121 came from. CAPTAIN DECISION 227a ADDS A SIXTH, is_mayhem_mode, so this ceiling was RE-MEASURED rather than assumed to survive it — 2026-08-05, through enumerateCreations against the deployed query: 51,691 bytes over 488 rows in the same five-wallet batch shape = 105.92 bytes/row, and 26,690 bytes over 252 rows for ONE wallet = 105.91. Both sit under 121, so the pinned value DOES NOT MOVE. TWO THINGS THE RE-MEASUREMENT CHANGED THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE NUMBER. (1) The two shapes agree to two decimals, so total_result_set_bytes is per-row with negligible per-response overhead at these sizes — which CONTRADICTS the stated cause of the older ~115 bytes/row five-column reading (28,699 bytes over 250 rows, one wallet), which this file attributed to overhead amortised over fewer rows. A 252-row read now lands at the same figure as a 488-row one, so that explanation does not hold, the 115 does not reproduce in this accounting, and it must not be carried forward. (2) THE HEADROOM IS NOW THINNER THAN ONE MORE COLUMN IS WORTH: 121 - 105.92 = 15.08 bytes, against an arithmetic worst case of ~23 for a single boolean column (a JSON key plus `false`). So this ceiling survives the sixth column and would NOT survive a seventh by arithmetic. A SEVENTH COLUMN MUST RE-MEASURE AND RAISE THIS VALUE rather than lean on a margin that is no longer there. It bounds the EXPORT half of the worst case: maxResultRows x this x (maxExecutionsPerRun + 1) reads at 20 credits/MB. RAISING maxResultRows OR ADDING A COLUMN MOVES THIS, and CREATION-DERIVED.md 8.2c owns every figure above.
justification.allowanceReserveCredits: 25 credits held back from every allowance reading before the plan is compared against it, and it exists because THE COUNTER LAGS. Measured on this account during the Dune evaluation: `credits_used` rose +6.0 while the evaluator was completely idle, and it lands in whole-credit jumps — so a reading understates spend, therefore OVERSTATES what remains, and a guard that spent to the last credit would be spending money the vendor has already taken. It also absorbs part of a second gap it cannot measure: the key is SHARED, so another holder may spend between our reading and our execution. NO MEASUREMENT FIXES THE MULTIPLE and it is stated rather than dressed up: 25 is ~4x the single observed drift and 1% of the free tier's 2,500. What would justify a value: a series of readings taken immediately before and after executions of known cost, which would price the lag distribution instead of one sample of it. The failure direction is the safe one — too large a reserve refuses a run that would have fitted, and this leg's refusal falls back to the RPC walk, which is slower rather than wrong.
justification.allowanceTightMultiple: 2. NOT A REFUSAL BAR — the threshold at which a run that WILL proceed prints a warning. A run whose worst case fits once but not twice may be the last one the period can afford, and an operator queueing heavier work behind it should learn that before the allowance is gone rather than from an HTTP 402 mid-run. NO MEASUREMENT BACKS THE 2, and here is what would: the distribution of Dune-spending runs per billing period, which does not exist because nothing here has yet run on a schedule. 2 is chosen as the smallest multiple that expresses 'this run is repeatable', which is the property that makes a failure recoverable.
justification.allowanceRequired: `true` — a run REFUSES the whole Dune leg when POST /usage cannot be read, rather than proceeding blind. NOT A MEASUREMENT, a policy, and it is the one the whole guard turns on: an unreadable balance is not headroom, and 'we could not see it' is the same evidence as 'it is empty'. The cost of being wrong is bounded and known — this leg falls back to the Solana RPC walk, which needs no Dune credential and is slower rather than wrong — while the cost of being wrong the other way is a billed multi-execution run that dies partway with neither a result nor the credits to retry. The reading itself is free (Dune documents /usage as a metadata endpoint consuming no credits) and is retried once, so a single transport hiccup does not reach this switch.
justification.refreshProbeByDefault: NOT A MEASUREMENT — a mode switch, and it is `false` because the probe is PARAMETERLESS and therefore has a cached answer that costs no execution at all. Re-executing it every run would spend the binding budget on a figure that moves by one row per second. `--dune-refresh-probe` makes it explicit, and staleness re-executes it anyway (see maxCoverageLagMs), so the default cannot silently publish a count over coverage nobody checked.
